title: My school and local features
objective: Name and locate my school and local features.
unit: My local place and the wider world
evidence: F: map check plus one independent location question.
success: Name my school in my chosen response mode.
Use a key to locate two features.
Show where one feature is in relation to the school.
career: A school caretaker uses a site plan to locate places and guide visitors. Practise giving a visitor one clear direction.
words: find and show where something is
something you can identify in a place
a mark that stands for something
the way from one place to another
a short distance away in this plan
tasks: Name one place you recognise near school.
Choose one route and answer four retrieval questions.
Point to the school symbol using the key.
Watch how I locate the school and park.
Match each symbol to the feature it represents.
Watch how I describe a route from school to the library.
Choose the direction from school to the library.
Name your school and locate two nearby features on your own plan.
Show one feature in relation to the school.
next: Arrival: use the key beside the four questions.
Starter: model the school symbol again or add the park.
I Do: trace the school and park on the plan.
We Do: match the symbols together.
I Do 2: trace the school-to-library route.
We Do 2: choose a direction and explain it.
Independent: draw your school and nearby features.
Exit: check one location without the model.
Next lesson: use a simple map or plan of a familiar place.
models: I read the key: a square marked S stands for school. I find S at the lower left. The triangle marked P is the park at the upper left. The park is above the school on this plan. I use the symbol and position together.

I start at S, the school. I follow the dashed route to L, the library. I move right across the page. My direction is: “From school, go right to the library.” The plan is a teaching example, so it does not tell us a safe walking route outside.

supported: Which place is for learning: school or river?
The key says S = school. What does S mean?
Read or point to the words after the equals sign.
Point to the right side of this page.
An adult can model left, then you show the opposite side.
The right side of the page.
Choose a natural feature: river or library.
A river is flowing water; a library is built by people.
standard: Name a place people visit near a school.
Think of a park, library, shop or bus stop.
Accept a suitable local place; check the actual locality with the adult.
Why does a map have a key?
To explain what the symbols mean.
A library is on the right of a school on a plan. Which way would you point?
Keep the plan the same way up.
Which is human-made: a river or a bus stop?
Human-made means people built or arranged it.
stretch: How could you check the name of your school?
Think of a sign, school document or a trusted adult.
Read the school sign or confirm with a trusted adult.
Why can the same square mean different things on different maps?
Symbols depend on the key; do not assume their meaning.
What must stay fixed when we say left or right on a plan?
Imagine turning the page upside down.
The orientation of the plan, or an agreed viewpoint.
Can a classroom plan prove a route is safe outside?
Think about roads, crossings and changes.
No. An adult must check the actual route and current conditions.

checks.question: Which symbol means park?
checks.feedback: The key shows P in a triangle for park. Read each map’s own key.

checks.question: From S to L, which direction crosses this page?
checks.feedback: The library is to the right of the school on this fixed plan.

independent: Name your school to the adult. Draw a school box. Add or point to two nearby features you know. Show one position with above, below, left or right. The adult may scribe your exact words.
Draw a simple plan of your school and two real nearby features. Add a key. Describe one feature’s position using left, right, near or far. Tell the adult which detail needs checking.

Draw and label a school plan with three local features and a key. Explain one position and how you would check it against the real place. Explain why this plan alone cannot confirm a safe walking route.
exit: On the teaching plan, point to the park in relation to the school.
The park is above the school on the page. Accept pointing or a directed adult response.
Name your school and describe where one real feature is on your plan.
School name and one plausible relative position, checked by the adult against the local setting.
Explain how the key and a position word together help someone find a feature.
The key identifies the feature; a position word tells the reader where to look.
misconception: A map is a view from above, not a picture of the front of a building. Keep the page orientation fixed before using left and right.
prep: Before teaching, confirm the school name and two familiar nearby features. Use the school’s approved local plan if available; otherwise make a shared plan from the classroom viewpoint. Do not ask for home addresses. The supplied fictional plan is for modelling; the independent response must transfer to the pupil’s actual school.
sources: Map skills context. Our S/P/L plan and symbols are original teaching graphics, not OS symbols.
Fictional diagram. No scale, real school location or safe route is asserted.
